implementation_notes: The classic C++ guard: one mutex-protected std::unordered_set whose insert() returns a pair whose .second is true only for the delivery that inserted the key - a single atomic claim instead of a separate contains()/insert() pair. Process-local and non-durable, so it fits only receivers that tolerate losing the seen-set on restart and that never run two instances against the same queue; the SQLite inbox variant is the durable counterpart. Values may carry an expiry timestamp so a sweep can enforce the retention window an unordered_set does not have.
pitfalls: std::unordered_set::insert is atomic only under the same mutex; a lock-free read path (count() then insert()) reintroduces the check-then-act race.
The set dies with the process and is per-process: with competing consumers each instance claims the same key independently.
No TTL exists for unordered_set entries - retention must be swept deliberately or the guard grows for the process lifetime.

variants.name: Durable SQLite inbox (INSERT OR IGNORE)
variants.implementation_notes: The durable realization: a claim table with a UNIQUE key column, where `INSERT OR IGNORE` plus sqlite3_changes() is the atomic claim and the business write joins the same transaction so a crash cannot leave effects without a marker. Choose it whenever redelivery can outlive the process or several processes consume the same queue; run BEGIN IMMEDIATE (or WAL plus busy retry) so concurrent claim attempts serialize at the database rather than in application code.
pitfalls: Committing the marker before the business write turns a crash into a lost message; keep both in one transaction.
SQLITE_BUSY from concurrent writers must be retried as a transient failure, never mistaken for a duplicate claim.
variants.idiom_name: SQLite unique key + INSERT OR IGNORE + sqlite3_changes()
